name: Metformin
route_note: oral tablet (immediate- or extended-release) or solution, with meals

discovery.by: Emil Werner and James Bell (synthesis); Jean Sterne (clinical use, 1957)
discovery.note: A guanidine derivative related to compounds in French lilac (Galega officinalis), a traditional remedy for diabetic symptoms.

tagline: The first-line pill for type 2 diabetes, descended from a medieval herbal remedy
summary: Metformin is a biguanide that lowers blood glucose mainly by reducing glucose production in the liver, without causing weight gain or hypoglycaemia on its own. It is the most widely prescribed glucose-lowering drug and is recommended first-line for type 2 diabetes in most guidelines.
mechanism: Metformin is taken up into hepatocytes by the organic cation transporter OCT1 and accumulates in mitochondria, where it mildly inhibits respiratory chain complex I (and, in some studies, mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase). The resulting change in cellular energy and redox state suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis.

The energy shift activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which contributes to reduced lipogenesis and improved insulin sensitivity, although part of the glucose-lowering effect is AMPK-independent. Metformin also acts in the gut, increasing glucose utilisation, GLP-1 secretion and altering the microbiome.
uses: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (monotherapy or combination, adults and children 10 years and older)
Prevention of type 2 diabetes in high-risk adults (guideline use)

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Emil Werner and James Bell synthesise dimethylbiguanide in Dublin.

history.title: Clinical introduction
history.detail: French physician Jean Sterne reports its use in diabetes and names it Glucophage ('glucose eater').

history.title: UK availability
history.detail: Metformin becomes available in the United Kingdom.

history.title: Phenformin withdrawn
history.detail: The related biguanide phenformin is withdrawn in the US because of lactic acidosis, delaying metformin's US entry.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: FDA approves Bristol-Myers Squibb's Glucophage in December 1994.

history.title: UKPDS
history.detail: The UK Prospective Diabetes Study reports reduced diabetes-related outcomes with metformin in overweight patients.

history.title: Diabetes Prevention Program
history.detail: Metformin reduces progression to diabetes by 31% versus placebo in high-risk adults (NEJM 2002).

history.title: Renal labelling eased
history.detail: FDA revises labelling to allow use with mild-to-moderate kidney impairment based on eGFR.

history.title: NDMA recalls
history.detail: FDA asks manufacturers to recall some extended-release metformin lots with excess N-nitrosodimethylamine.

pk.excretion: unchanged in urine by tubular secretion

serious: vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
safety.boxed_warning: Lactic acidosis: postmarketing cases, sometimes fatal, especially with renal impairment, hypoxia, excess alcohol, contrast imaging or hepatic impairment.

facts: Metformin is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.
It is being studied in ageing research (the proposed TAME trial).
Metformin is not metabolised and is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
